source: Barbieri, Miller-Cotto, Clerjuste, Chawla (2023) A meta-analysis of the worked examples effect on mathematics performance (published abstract, via search summary)
finding: Worked examples give a medium average gain on maths outcomes. Correct examples alone beat incorrect-only or mixed correct plus incorrect examples. Adding self-explanation prompts moderated the effect in the NEGATIVE direction. The effect held for both practice and first learning.
numbers: Overall g = 0.48 (RVE, p = 0.01). 8,033 abstracts screened, 43 articles (41 experimental, 2 quasi-experimental), 55 studies, 181 effect sizes.
limits: Publisher full text not readable this session (Springer paywall redirect); numbers come from a search-engine summary of the abstract. Maths only. Treat the self-explanation sign as unverified until the paper is read.
agent_relevance: Baseline expectation for a subgoal library: roughly half a standard deviation from showing solved cases. Do not assume that forcing explanation on top of the example helps.

source: Clerjuste, Chawla, Barbieri, Miller-Cotto (2022) Meta-analysis of the worked examples effect on mathematics performance (conference poster, earlier analysis)
finding: Earlier run of the same meta-analysis found a smaller effect and NO significant moderator. The authors concluded the effect is robust to design, age and content area.
numbers: 40 articles, 49 studies (46 experimental, 3 quasi), 185 effect sizes from -1.80 to 4.66; 41 negative, 144 positive. g = 0.43, 95% CI 0.31 to 0.55. I-squared = 94.46%. Moderators tested: type of example, administration format, grade level, content area; none significant. 32 articles used correct examples, 7 incorrect, 4 faded.
quote: Learners who study worked examples improve almost half of a standard deviation (g = .43)
limits: Poster, not the final paper. Final paper moved to g = 0.48 with moderators that did differ (see b01), so moderator findings are unstable across analysis versions. Heterogeneity is huge: the mean hides effects from -1.8 to +4.7.
agent_relevance: Treat the average as an expectation, not a promise. Very high heterogeneity means per-task ablation in our own agent is required.

source: Barbieri et al. (2023), IES 2007 practice guide comparison (from poster)
finding: The 2007 IES practice guide rated interleaving worked examples with problem solving as moderate evidence. The poster notes only 5 of 40 included articles were published by 2007, so the later evidence base is mostly new and agrees with the guide.
numbers: 5 of 40 articles dated 2007 or earlier.
limits: Poster claim; not independently checked against the IES guide.
agent_relevance: Supports interleaving a stored solution with a live attempt rather than showing only solutions.

source: Sweller (2023) The development of cognitive load theory: replication failures and theory integration
finding: The original worked-example effect (algebra, Sweller and Cooper 1985; Cooper and Sweller 1987) FAILED to replicate with geometry and with physics kinematics for several years. Cause found later: split attention. Geometry and kinematics examples need the learner to match text to a diagram. When text and diagram were physically integrated, the effect came back.
numbers: Qualitative account, no new numbers. Algebra: multiple experiments positive. Geometry and kinematics: no worked-example advantage until split attention was removed (Tarmizi and Sweller 1988; Ward and Sweller 1990).
quote: each failure to replicate, rather than being a negative, contributed to theory development
limits: Author is the theory's founder, reports his own history; no effect sizes given. Direct replication failures here were across domains, not same-materials repeats.
agent_relevance: A stored example helps only if it is self-contained. A subgoal-library entry that refers to a figure or earlier text that is not in the prompt is a split-attention trap.

source: Sweller (2023), second and third failures: split-attention and redundancy
finding: Integrating text and diagram then failed to help when the diagram was already self-sufficient. This is the redundancy effect. So adding more explanation to a clear example can hurt or do nothing.
numbers: No numbers; blood-flow diagram example.
limits: Narrative history, no effect sizes.
agent_relevance: Do not pad stored examples with prose that restates the steps. Keep entries minimal when the steps are already readable.

source: Sweller (2023), element interactivity and expertise reversal section
finding: Cognitive load theory now explains the worked-example effect and its reversal by element interactivity: examples help when the task has many interacting elements for this learner. For learners who already know the material, the same example is redundant.
numbers: Qualitative; no sample sizes.
limits: Explanation after the fact; the theory has been criticised as hard to falsify, which this paper's own framing (every failure absorbed as theory growth) illustrates.
agent_relevance: Show examples when the agent's problem has many interacting parts. For easy items of a known class, skip them (saves tokens).

source: Wikipedia (accessed 2026) Worked-example effect: study table (secondary, summarised by fetch tool)
finding: Page lists boundary conditions: expertise reversal (Kalyuga, Chandler, Sweller 2000, 2001; Kalyuga et al. 2001 JEP), no reversal in less structured domain (Nievelstein et al. 2013, legal cases, novice and advanced law students both gained in efficiency), one vs three examples per type no difference on sorting (Quilici and Mayer 1996), half-worked equal to fully worked (Paas 1992), two examples with a harder second give transfer (Reed and Bolstad 1991), three fading stages better than one (Pillay 1994).
numbers: Page itself gives no sample sizes or effect sizes.
limits: Encyclopaedia page, secondary; several citations flagged as unverified on the page. Primary papers were not opened. Used only as a map to follow.
agent_relevance: Maps directly onto the schema question set: one vs several examples, partial vs full, fading. All need primary-source numbers before use.

source: Wikipedia page, Schwonke et al. (2009) and van Gog, Kester, Paas (2011) as listed
finding: Geometry Cognitive Tutor: worked examples cut learning time in Exp. 1, and Exp. 2 replicated the efficiency gain and added deeper conceptual understanding. Troubleshooting circuits: example-only and example-then-problem beat problem-then-example and problem-only, with lower mental effort.
numbers: No numbers on the page.
limits: Secondary summary only.
agent_relevance: Order matters: show the example first, then ask for a solve. Problem-first loses the benefit.

source: McLaren, Lim, Koedinger (2008) and Stoich studies, as summarised on LearnLab wiki
finding: In three stoichiometry tutor studies, alternating worked examples with tutored problems did NOT raise learning, but cut time on task. So the effect here was efficiency only.
numbers: Study 1 N = 63, Study 2 N = 60, Study 3 N = 81 total. Learning gains: no significant effect of worked examples in Studies 1-3; all conditions improved pretest to posttest. Time: examples group used significantly less time, 21% less overall. Study 4 retention results not reported.
limits: Wiki summary with no means, p-values or effect sizes. Tutored problem solving is a strong control with hints, so little room for a learning gain.
agent_relevance: Against a strong support condition (hints on), examples bought speed not accuracy. For an agent: examples may save tokens and steps at equal accuracy, which is a fair result to report.

source: Miller-Cotto and Medrano (2026) Does working memory moderate the effect of fading on maths performance? Br J Educ Psychol
finding: Sixth graders, geometry homework in ASSISTments. Fading beat problem solving; plain worked examples with self-explanation prompts did not. Working memory did not moderate; prior knowledge did moderate fading.
numbers: N = 114, four conditions: worked example plus self-explanation, fading plus self-explanation, fading alone, problem solving only. Pre-to-post Hedges g: fading 1.08, fading plus self-explanation 0.93, worked example plus self-explanation 0.32, business as usual 0.24. Regression vs business as usual: fading beta = .60, p = .03; worked example beta = .01, p = .96; fading plus self-explanation beta .50, p = .08. Working memory by condition interaction ps > .50.
limits: Small groups (about 21 to 33 per cell), pre-test imbalance (business-as-usual differed from fading, p = .04), multiple imputation, and g is within-condition pre/post change, not a between-group effect size. Randomised but homework setting.
agent_relevance: Failed replication of the plain worked-example benefit in a modern classroom study, with fading as the winner. Supports fading from solved steps into own work in the subgoal library.

source: Miller-Cotto and Medrano (2026), self-explanation arm
finding: Adding self-explanation prompts did not help here: fading plus prompts (g = 0.93) was not better than fading alone (g = 1.08), and worked example plus prompts (g = 0.32) barely beat business as usual (0.24).
numbers: Pre-post g: fading 1.08 vs fading plus self-explanation 0.93. Posttest means (column order inferred from the pretest-imbalance text): business as usual 59.08, worked example plus SE 53.71, fading 63.28, fading plus SE 62.36.
limits: Between-condition differences in posttest were not significant (ps > .05); table column labels in the extracted text were partly lost, so cell assignment is by order.
agent_relevance: Agrees with the negative self-explanation moderator in b01. Prompting a model to explain every example may be wasted tokens.

source: Stone, Fish, Chernyak, Guadalupe, Cordes (2026) Role of worked examples in early maths learning, J Intell
finding: Preschoolers watched correct or incorrect division strategies and explained them. Both helped versus a baseline task, mainly for the youngest children on the hardest, novel trials. Children who spontaneously named the process did better than those who named the outcome.
numbers: N = 201 children, ages 4.01 to 6.96 (M 5.57). Dissimilar block, large set: main effect of condition F(2,191) = 8.95, p < .001, partial eta-squared 0.09, correct and incorrect better than baseline. Similar block: only marginal condition by age effects (p about .07 to .08). 5-year-olds large set similar block: correct M 0.09, incorrect 0.19, baseline 1.08 deviation (lower is better).
limits: Video-based, no delay test, no effect for medium set sizes (ps > .21), many marginal results. Correct and incorrect did not differ, so cannot say which element helped.
agent_relevance: Both correct and incorrect worked cases carried benefit; a library of failed-then-fixed subgoals may be as useful as only clean ones. Process talk beat outcome talk: store the procedure, not the answer.

source: Wang, Li, Liu (2026) Boundary conditions of collaborative learning using worked examples, Front Psychol
finding: Studying worked examples with a partner helped only for high prior knowledge learners on high-complexity tasks. No stable benefit for low prior knowledge, none for far transfer. Collaborators reported lower load.
numbers: N = 134 fifth graders, 2 (prior knowledge) x 2 (task complexity, within) x 2 (individual vs collaborative). Near transfer: prior knowledge F(1,130) = 87.30, partial eta-squared .402; learning condition F(1,130) = 4.62, p < .05, eta-sq .034; three-way interaction F(1,130) = 6.07, p < .05, eta-sq .045. Far transfer: no effect of condition or interactions.
limits: Prior knowledge was induced experimentally, task-specific, one school culture (China), maths only. Effect on condition main effect small.
agent_relevance: Two-agent or debate setups over a stored example help only when each agent can already partly do the task. Do not expect multi-agent review to fix a weak base.

source: Question prompts vs worked examples in primary science, Behav Sci (2026)
finding: Worked examples and question prompts both produced large pre-post gains in primary science. Worked examples were equal on overall knowledge, and better on one argumentation sub-skill.
numbers: N = 34 per group (68 total). Knowledge: QP d = 1.31, WE d = 1.32, group main effect p = .468, time by group p = .524. One sub-skill: QP pre-post d = 0.83, WE d = 0.98. A second sub-skill: QP d = 1.02, WE d = 1.40; posttest WE higher than QP, t(66) = -2.54, p = .014, d = 0.62.
limits: Small N; pre-post d inflated by practice and by no true control; baseline difference at pretest p = .051, d = 0.48 on that sub-skill. Not a worked example vs unguided comparison.
agent_relevance: In an ill-structured science task, a model answer matched question scaffolding. Suggests examples are not strictly limited to algorithmic domains.

source: Min et al. (2022) Rethinking the role of demonstrations: what makes in-context learning work?
finding: Randomly replacing the labels in few-shot demonstrations barely hurts accuracy. What matters is label space, input distribution and format.
numbers: 12 models including GPT-3; classification and multi-choice tasks; random-label demos stay close to gold-label demos and far above no demos (figure-level results).
limits: Classification and multiple-choice only; did not test multi-step reasoning. Later work disputed generality for reasoning.
agent_relevance: A stored example mostly teaches format and domain, not content. Parallel to human finding that surface structure of examples cues schema.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Towards understanding chain-of-thought prompting: what matters
finding: Invalid reasoning in CoT demonstrations keeps 80 to 90 percent of CoT accuracy. Relevance to the query and correct order of steps matter much more than validity.
numbers: text-davinci-002, GSM8K answer accuracy: standard 15.4, CoT 48.5, invalid reasoning 39.5 (81 percent of CoT), no coherence 23.1, no relevance 11.0. Bamboogle: standard 20.6, CoT 45.2, invalid 39.4, no relevance 23.9.
limits: Older model, GSM8K 800-item sample, handwritten corruptions; strong modern models may behave differently.
agent_relevance: Matches human finding that example structure beats example correctness. Keep stored subgoal examples relevant and ordered; small errors cost less than irrelevance.

source: Wang et al. (2023), error analysis and coherence ablations
finding: Destroying coherence of language templates hurts a lot, while destroying coherence of bridging objects hurts less. Models that copy the template's logic from an unrelated example score near the no-example baseline.
numbers: GSM8K intermediate F1: CoT 48.3, no relevance 11.9, no coherence 29.4. Answer accuracy: no relevance 11.0 vs standard 15.4, so relevant structure is the entire gain.
limits: Intrinsic evaluation depends on a rationale parser; one model family.
agent_relevance: Retrieval of a relevant class matters more than example quality. Retrieval errors will cost more than imperfect examples.

source: Madaan and Yazdanbakhsh (2022) Text and patterns: for effective chain of thought it takes two to tango
finding: Counterfactual prompts show factual patterns in CoT examples are nearly immaterial. Intermediate steps mostly tell the model which symbols to replicate, not how to solve.
numbers: Four tasks, three models (PaLM, GPT-3, Codex); only one component of the prompt (symbols, patterns, text) altered at a time.
limits: Abstract-level claims read; per-condition numbers not extracted here. Older models.
agent_relevance: Warns that an example's apparent benefit may be a format effect, not skill transfer. Control for this with format-only exemplars.

source: Mishra and Thakkar (2023) Stress testing chain-of-thought prompting for large language models (course report)
finding: Wrong values in CoT demonstrations cause large drops, while wrong order or wrong operators hurt much less. Qualifies the idea that only structure matters, at least for numbers.
numbers: GPT-3 text-davinci-002, temperature 0.6, tasks ASDiv, GSM8K, SVAMP, MAWPS; exact accuracies not extracted.
limits: Student course report, not peer reviewed; single model.
agent_relevance: Numeric values in a stored worked solution are load-bearing. Do not shuffle or paraphrase numbers.

source: Cheng et al. (2026) Revisiting chain-of-thought prompting: zero-shot can be stronger than few-shot
finding: For strong instruction-tuned models (Qwen2.5 series), adding CoT exemplars does not beat zero-shot CoT. The exemplars mostly align output format. Even exemplars written by a stronger model (Qwen2.5-Max, DeepSeek-R1) did not help.
numbers: Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct: GSM8K 8-shot 95.75 vs zero-shot 91.58, but zero-shot after fixing answer-format scoring 95.83. MATH 8-shot 81.30 vs zero-shot 81.64. Base model: GSM8K 90.52 vs 84.69; MATH 75.82 vs 70.60. LSAT-LR Qwen2.5-72B-it few-shot 41.55 vs zero-shot 84.65; LSAT-RC few-shot 36.92 vs zero-shot 84.24. Reported about 100 truncation or repetition errors out of 1,319 GSM8K questions.
limits: Maths and LSAT only; Qwen family; models tend to ignore exemplars. Base models still lean on exemplars (format).
agent_relevance: Expertise reversal for models: strong models gain nothing from generic examples. Test our library per model and per class; expect gains only where the model fails alone.

source: De Wynter (2026) Is in-context learning learning?
finding: At many shots, accuracy becomes insensitive to exemplar distribution, model, prompt style and wording. ICL deduces patterns from regularities in the prompt; CoT is most distribution-sensitive.
numbers: Best-of-average accuracy is reached around 50 to 100 shots in the paper's settings; CoT peaked fast then fell.
limits: Large synthetic and formal-task battery; not human-style worked examples; detailed per-task numbers not extracted here.
agent_relevance: Piling on examples does not teach a new skill. Few well-chosen entries in the library, not a long dump.

source: Agarwal et al. (2024) Many-shot in-context learning
finding: Many solved examples beat few across many tasks; model-generated solutions (Reinforced ICL) or problems without any solutions (Unsupervised ICL) can match human-written ones on reasoning. Too many examples can hurt.
numbers: MATH500: plain ICL peaks near 125 examples then declines; Reinforced ICL plateaus near 25 examples, about 5 percent higher than ground-truth ICL, no sharp drop later. 4-shot Minerva prompt: 55.7 percent MATH500, 90.6 percent GSM8K. The paper also notes a performance degradation at 250 shots in one task.
limits: Gemini 1.5 Pro with million-token context; strong math pretraining may make solutions redundant (authors' own caveat).
agent_relevance: Model-written solved cases can replace human ones (supports an agent that builds its own library). Cap library size; diminishing and negative returns appear.

source: Yasunaga et al. (2024) Large language models as analogical reasoners
finding: Having the model write its own relevant solved examples before answering beats 0-shot CoT and often manual few-shot CoT.
numbers: GPT-3.5-turbo GSM8K: 5-shot CoT 75.0 to about 77.8 with self-generated exemplars; MATH about 33.0 to 37.3 (table layout partly garbled in extraction, treat as approximate). Number of self-generated exemplars: K = 1 gives 76.1 GSM8K and 34.8 MATH; K = 3 to 5 gives about 77.3 to 77.8 and 37.0 to 37.3. Codeforces GPT-3.5 Acc@1 15 percent vs GPT-4 16 percent.
limits: Gains are small on GSM8K (about 1 to 3 points) and larger for weaker or older models. Single-example prompts underperform.
agent_relevance: Self-generated worked examples are a cheap library fill. One example is brittle; use three. Value is largest on weaker models.

source: Wang, Mao, Fried, Neubig (2024) Agent Workflow Memory
finding: Inducing reusable workflows from past successful trajectories and showing them to a web agent raised success, and helped most when train and test tasks were far apart.
numbers: WebArena: 51.1 percent relative gain over the BrowserGym baseline, 12.0 absolute points; WebArena overall success 35.5 percent (GPT-4, temperature 0). Mind2Web: 24.6 percent relative step success gain. Beat SteP (human-written workflows) by 7.6 percent relative. Gains over baselines grew from 8.9 to 14.0 absolute points as train-test gap widened. Authors warn incorrect induced workflows can degrade performance.
limits: Web navigation, GPT-4 only; online variant risks storing wrong workflows. Not a pure worked-example test: workflows are abstracted, not full solutions.
agent_relevance: Closest direct analogue of our subgoal library; supports it, and flags error propagation as the main risk.

source: Cross-study contrast: human worked-example moderators vs LLM exemplar moderators (synthesis of b01 to b24)
finding: Humans: examples help novices, fade for experts, need integrated format, plain examples sometimes fail in modern classroom trials. LLMs: examples help weak or format-poor models, add nothing for strong ones, and relevance and ordering beat correctness.
numbers: Pairs: expertise reversal (Kalyuga) vs Cheng 2026 zero-shot parity; split attention vs Wang 2023 relevance ablation; efficiency-not-learning (McLaren, 21 percent time cut) vs Cheng format-alignment effect.
limits: Synthesis by the agent, not a study. Cross-species analogy untested.
agent_relevance: Design rule for the agent: gate example insertion on whether the model fails alone, use few relevant self-contained examples, then fade to a bare subgoal cue.

source: Sweller (2023), theory-based caution on all replication claims
finding: Author argues contradictory results often reflect missing variables, not bad data. This means a failed replication of the worked-example effect should be read as a clue to a moderator, but also that any result can be explained away after the fact.
numbers: No numbers. Distinguishes direct from conceptual replication (Plucker and Makel 2021).
limits: Self-referential defence of the theory; no preregistered test of the added moderators shown.
agent_relevance: For our ablations, preregister the moderator (model strength, example integration, domain structure) before running, so a null is informative.
